conversation.content:
Hi there—I’m Claire, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’m here to help you settle into motherhood by checking in on how you’ve been feeling. We’ll use a short, well-trusted tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply ten questions about the past seven days, and it helps us spot anything from normal “baby blues” to something that might need extra support. Everything you share stays between us unless you tell me someone is in danger. There are no right or wrong answers—just your honest experience. Ready to begin?

First question: Over the past seven days, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, even in small moments?

Honestly? I can still laugh a little—maybe when my husband sends me a silly meme or when the baby makes those funny milk-drunk faces—but it feels kind of forced. Most of the time the laughter just doesn’t bubble up the way it used to, and even when I do chuckle, it fades fast and I’m right back to feeling heavy.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Mostly just here and there—maybe a quick smile or a half-laugh once a day, if that. It doesn’t feel natural or last long.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not very often. I used to get excited about little plans—grabbing coffee with a friend, a walk with the stroller, even just a quiet shower—but lately it all feels like one more chore. Every now and then I’ll think “maybe tomorrow will feel better,” but the actual looking-forward feeling barely shows up.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that one hits. When the baby won’t settle or I can’t figure out what he needs, I keep thinking I must be doing something wrong—like a “good mom” would know how to fix it. Even spilling a little pumped milk or running late for a pediatric visit turns into this loop of “I’m failing him.” It’s not every second, but it’s been most days this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly picture him stopping breathing, or worry the car-seat buckle isn’t tight enough, or imagine dropping him—even when nothing’s happening. I know in my head it’s unlikely, but the thoughts just start spinning and I can’t shut them off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A few times—like last night when I was trying to fall asleep and suddenly my heart started racing and I felt like I couldn’t get a full breath. Nothing set it off; the house was quiet, baby was asleep, but for a couple of minutes I felt like something awful was about to happen. It passed, but it left me shaky and on edge the rest of the night.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah... most days. Between feedings, diapers, trying to sleep, and the house piling up, it feels like I'm drowning a little. I manage to get through the essentials, but it's like I'm constantly behind and can't catch my breath.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes. I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps circling through everything I might be doing wrong or what could go wrong with the baby. It takes me a long time to drift off, and when I do I wake up again with my heart pounding. I’d say I’ve had trouble falling or staying asleep on four or five nights this week.
I have felt sad or miserable
Pretty much every day. It’s not crying-all-day bad, but there’s this steady sadness that sits on me like a weight. Even when nothing specific is wrong, I still feel down and kind of empty.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Once was after a rough night when the baby wouldn’t latch and I felt completely useless. The other time was yesterday—my mom called to check in, asked how I was doing, and I just lost it on the phone. Both times the tears came out of nowhere and I couldn’t stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s crossed my mind… just fleeting, scary flashes. Like, I’ll be standing at the top of the stairs holding the baby and suddenly picture myself falling on purpose, or I’ll see the kitchen scissors and get this quick image of doing something awful. I’ve never made a plan and I don’t want to die—I just want the pressure and sadness to stop—but yeah, those thoughts have popped up once or twice in the past week and they shake me.

I hear how heavy each day feels right now-how the joy that used to come easily now slips through your fingers, replaced by a steady sadness, constant worry, and exhausting self-blame. You're working so hard to care for your baby while battling intrusive fears, sleepless nights, and frightening thoughts you never asked for. Your honesty about these feelings is courageous, and it confirms you deserve immediate help and relief.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Response indicates marked reduction in ability to laugh, matching "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost no anticipatory enjoyment, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient clearly describes frequent self-blame ('most days this week', 'keep thinking I must be doing something wrong'), matching 'Yes, some of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily intrusive, uncontrollable worries about infant safety with no objective trigger, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes discrete episodes of sudden, unexplained panic with physical symptoms (racing heart, breathlessness, dread) that happened "a few times," aligning with "Yes, sometimes."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "most days" and "drowning," indicating frequent difficulty coping, aligning with "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports sleep difficulty on most nights (4-5/7) directly linked to unhappiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports daily sadness and emptiness, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes this week triggered by feeling overwhelmed and unsupported, aligning with "Yes, quite often" (score 2).</sym>)
**Reasoning:** With an EPDS of 23 and endorsement of Item 10 (fleeting self-harm images), the patient meets screening criteria for probable <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. She reports <sym>daily sadness</sym>, <sym>anhedonia</sym>, <sym>excessive guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep-onset insomnia</sym>, <sym>panic episodes</sym>, and <sym>intrusive anxious thoughts</sym>-all aligning with DSM-5 criteria. Safety concern is heightened by <quote>I've never made a plan and I don't want to die-I just want the pressure and sadness to stop</quote>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange same-day urgent appointment with <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal psychiatrist for full evaluation and safety plan
2. Call a 24/7 crisis line or go to the nearest emergency department if self-harm thoughts intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Share these EPDS results with your obstetrician or midwife so they can expedite referral and coordinate care
4. Ask a trusted adult to stay with you and help with infant care while treatment is organised
5. Begin basic self-care: accept help with housework, aim for brief outdoor walks, and eat small frequent meals
6. Consider evidence-based therapies such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>CBT</med> tailored for postpartum depression
7. Discuss with your doctor whether an antidepressant compatible with breastfeeding might be appropriate
8. Schedule follow-up EPDS in 2 weeks to monitor progress after interventions are started
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note  
Date: [Today’s date]  
Source: 10-item self-report; responses consistent with moderate–severe symptom endorsement.

<sym>Symptoms endorsed</sym>  
- Persistent low mood, emptiness, daily crying spells (Q8, Q9)  
- Marked anhedonia; minimal pleasure or anticipatory enjoyment (Q1, Q2)  
- Excessive guilt / self-blame regarding parenting performance (Q3)  
- intrusive anxious thoughts & nightly worry ruminations (Q4)  
- Panic-type episodes (racing heart, breathlessness) without clear precipitant (Q5)  
- Sleep-onset and maintenance insomnia linked to mood concerns (Q7)  
- Subjective sense of “drowning,” unable to catch up (Q6)  
- Fleeting passive self-harm images (no plan, intent, or desire to die) (Q10)

<med>Risk indicators</med>  
1. Probable major depressive episode (peripartum onset) – multiple core criteria met (low mood, anhedonia, guilt, fatigue, sleep disturbance).  
2. Comorbid anxiety symptoms meeting clinical threshold – generalized & panic features.  
3. Safety concern: presence of unwanted self-harm cognitions; no protective factors detailed.

<med>Overall screening impression</sym>  
Responses place patient above conventional cut-off for probable postpartum depression with co-occurring anxiety. Passive self-harm thoughts warrant immediate safety assessment. Recommend expedited referral to perinatal mental health specialist and same-day safety planning with PCP or emergency resource.
